To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the work done by a voter can be reduced to essentially minimal size, while keeping the work done by tallying servers on a practical and reasonable level.

(a) the work load of the clients can be reduced to a minimum, while (b) the work load on tally servers can be kept within practical limits and (c) the security of the voting scheme can be increased to allow for monitoring of all clients used by voters to cast their ballots, while (d) a trusted party has to be introduced to carry out registration.

(1) the work done by voters is not necessarily a good measure of the overall complexity of a voting scheme and (2) the work done at the client side is a good measure for the overall complexity of an election.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to design a voting scheme that minimizes the amount of work done by voters while keeping the work on the tallying servers at a reasonable level.
finding the right balance of security, privacy, and efficiency for various voting schemes.
the question of how much work should be delegated from the voter to the tallying servers in an online election.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no free lunches.
there are no free lunches in voting schemes.
there is no free lunch in online elections.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that there is a trade off between the amount of work that voters and the tally servers must perform.
we show how a client can be made to do almost nothing while a server can be made to work very hard.
the trade offs we present allow us to achieve better security and/or efficiency in online elections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a wide range of possible tradeoffs between the work load on voters and the work load on servers.
, in some settings, it is better to do more work at the server end than on the client end.

the trade offs we present can be used to design voting protocols with different security and performance characteristics, and that the design space for such trade offs is much larger than has previously been considered.
